```{r}
#| label: setup

source("../_common.R")
```

I've finally added [`webR`](https://docs.r-wasm.org/webr/latest/) and [`shinyelectron`](https://r-pkg.thecoatlessprofessor.com/shinyelectron/) chapters to my [Shiny App-Packages](https://mjfrigaard.github.io/shiny-app-pkgs/) text (under the [Deploy section](https://mjfrigaard.github.io/shiny-app-pkgs/deploy.html)). 

* [webR chapter](https://mjfrigaard.github.io/shiny-app-pkgs/webr.html) runs the app in the user's browser
* [shinyelectron chapter](https://mjfrigaard.github.io/shiny-app-pkgs/shinyelectron.html) packages it as a desktop installer

In this post I'll cover what each chapter does with `sap` (the book's app-package), and a few of the problems I encountered along the way.

## Where does the app run?

Every deployment in the earlier book chapters (Connect Cloud, Docker, GitHub Actions) needs a server. These two chapters move R (and the app) onto the user's computer.

The diagram below shows where R runs in each case:

```{mermaid}

%%| fig-align: 'center'

    Pkg -->|"i. deploy"| RS
```

The chapters build on each other: The `shinyelectron` desktop chapter reuses the launcher from the `webR` browser chapter, and the Linux build depends on the `WebAssembly` binary we set up for the browser.

## `webR`: the app in a browser tab

[`webR`](https://docs.r-wasm.org/webr/latest/) is R compiled to [WebAssembly](https://webassembly.org/), a binary format that modern browsers run at near native speed. [`shinylive`](https://posit-dev.github.io/r-shinylive/) bundles a Shiny app, `webR`, and the app's packages into a folder of static files. A static file host is just a web server that hands out files without running any code. GitHub Pages or Netlify can serve the app.

After the first download, every click stays in the browser.

### What the browser doesnt't do

The browser takes on the server's job, but it can't do *all* of it. In my opinion, these trade-offs matter most:

* The first time the app loads, the browser downloads `webR` and every package before the app appears.
* All the code and data go to the browser, so never include credentials.
* You can't call on system tools or downloads (i.e., `system()` calls fail, `sass::font_google()` needs `local = FALSE`)  
* Temporary files like logs will disappear when the tab closes  

### Every package needs a binary

`webR` can't install packages from source, so each package in `Imports` needs a `WebAssembly` binary. The chapter checks `DESCRIPTION` against the [`webR` repository](https://repo.r-wasm.org):

```{r}
#| eval: false
#| code-fold: false
wasm_pkgs <- available.packages(
  contriburl = "https://repo.r-wasm.org/bin/emscripten/contrib/4.6"
)
base_pkgs <- rownames(installed.packages(priority = "base"))
imports <- read.dcf("DESCRIPTION", fields = "Imports")
imports <- trimws(strsplit(imports, ",")[[1]])
imports <- imports[imports != ""]
setdiff(imports, c(rownames(wasm_pkgs), base_pkgs))
```

An empty result (`character(0)`) means every dependency has a binary.

`sap` itself isn't on CRAN, so it has no binary. [R-universe](https://r-universe.dev/) builds one on each push. Setting it up takes a `<username>.r-universe.dev` repository, a `packages.json` file, and the R-universe GitHub app.

```{r}
#| label: co_box_r_universe
#| echo: false
#| results: asis
#| eval: true
co_box(
  color = "r",
  header = "Install the GitHub app first",
  contents = "Nothing builds until the R-universe GitHub app is installed. Use the installation link, not the repository settings.")
```

We then install `sap` from the universe, because `shinylive` uses each installed package's source to find its binary.

### A launcher, not `launch_app()`

`shinylive` exports a folder with an `app.R` file, not a package. The chapter adds a small launcher in `inst/webr/app.R`:

```{r}
#| eval: false
#| code-fold: false
library(shiny)
library(sap)

shinyApp(
  ui = movies_ui(bslib = TRUE),
  server = movies_server
)
```

The launcher returns a Shiny app object instead of calling the standalone app function (`launch_app()`). We use `shinyApp()` in `inst/webr/app.R` because `shiny::runApp()` starts a server and blocks the R session. The `library(sap)` call above is also important because `shinylive` scans `app.R` for `library()` calls to decide which binaries to bundle.

Exporting and previewing take two lines:

```{r}
#| eval: false
#| code-fold: false
shinylive::export(appdir = "inst/webr", destdir = "_site")
httpuv::runStaticServer("_site")
```

Opening `_site/index.html` directly won't work, because `webR` needs its files served over HTTP.

## `shinyelectron`: the app as a desktop program

Some users need the app as a program they install. They might work offline, or their organization might block unknown websites. [Electron](https://www.electronjs.org/) is a framework for desktop programs built with web technologies; an Electron app is just a web browser with a single page. [`shinyelectron`](https://r-pkg.thecoatlessprofessor.com/shinyelectron/) wraps a Shiny app in Electron, so the user never sees a browser or a URL.

### Choosing a runtime strategy

The app still needs R, and `shinyelectron` offers five ways to provide it. Each strategy trades installer size against what the user's computer needs:

| Strategy | The installer ships | The user needs |
|:---|:---|:---|
| `shinylive` | Electron and a `webR` bundle | nothing |
| `bundled` | Electron and a portable copy of R | nothing |
| `auto-download` | Electron and a downloader | internet on first launch |
| `system` | Electron only | R installed |
| `container` | Electron and a container setup | Docker or Podman |

The chapter uses `bundled` for macOS and Windows, which installs `sap` from local source. Portable R only exists for those two platforms, and `bundled` can't cross-build.

### The `electron/` folder

The package itself doesn't change. All the desktop code lives in an `electron/` folder: the same launcher `app.R` from the webR chapter, a `_shinyelectron.yml` configuration file, and a `build.R` script. The configuration file holds the setting I found most useful:

```yaml
dependencies:
  r:
    local_packages:
      - "../.."
```

`local_packages` installs `sap` from the package root, which is how a `bundled` app gets a package that isn't on CRAN. The CRAN release of `shinyelectron` (0.2.1) doesn't support this field yet, so the chapter installs the development version from GitHub.

### Building the `.dmg`

The build script checks the system with `sitrep_shinyelectron()`, validates the app with `app_check()`, and calls `export()`. On an Intel Mac, the result is a `.dmg` of about 256 MB, most of it portable R.

Most of the build warnings are harmless. The `NB` notes are worth fixing: `sap` uses the native pipe, so `R CMD build` raised `Depends` to R 4.1.0.

```{r}
#| label: co_box_rprofile
#| echo: false
#| results: asis
#| eval: true
co_box(
  color = "r",
  header = "Your `.Rprofile` comes along",
  contents = "The bundled R reads `~/.Rprofile`. If it calls a package the app doesn't include, the build fails. Wrap those calls in `requireNamespace()`.")
```

For Windows, a GitHub Actions matrix runs [`shiny-to-electron`](https://github.com/coatless-actions/shiny-to-electron) on macOS and Windows runners.

### Building the `.deb`

The Linux build took the most work. I use Pop!_OS (an Ubuntu-flavored Linux distro), and `shinyelectron` will only build an `.AppImage` on Linux. `bundled` isn't an option either, because there's no portable R for Linux.

I found a fix by combining both chapters: The `shinylive` strategy runs `sap` with `webR` inside the Electron window, which uses the R-universe binary from the `webR` chapter. `export()` builds the `.AppImage` and leaves an Electron project behind. The build script then edits that project's `package.json` and rebuilds it with `electron-builder`:

```{mermaid}
%%| fig-width: 6
%%| fig-align: 'center'
%%{init: {'theme': 'base', 'themeVariables': { 'fontFamily': 'monospace', "darkMode":false}}}%%
flowchart TD
    Start(["<code>electron/build.R</code>"])
    Export("<code>export()</code> converts the app<br>to shinylive and builds Electron")
    AppImage[/".AppImage"/]
    Project[("<code>electron-app/</code><br>Electron project")]
    Edit("Add the <code>deb</code> target,<br>homepage, and maintainer")
    Builder("<code>electron-builder</code><br>packages the project")
    Deb[/".deb"/]

    Start -->|"i. export"| Export
    Export --> AppImage
    Export --> Project
    Project -->|"ii. edit package.json"| Edit
    Edit -->|"iii. npx electron-builder"| Builder
    Builder --> Deb

    style Start fill:#FFFFFF,color:#000000,stroke:#333
    style Export fill:#4CBB9D,color:#FFFFFF,rx:5,ry:5
    style Edit fill:#4CBB9D,color:#FFFFFF,rx:5,ry:5
    style Builder fill:#4CBB9D,color:#FFFFFF,rx:5,ry:5
```

The edit adds three fields, because `electron-builder` refuses to build a `.deb` without a homepage and a maintainer:

```{r}
#| eval: false
#| code-fold: false
pkg <- jsonlite::read_json(pkg_json)
pkg$homepage <- "https://github.com/mjfrigaard/sap"
pkg$build$linux$target <- list("AppImage", "deb")
pkg$build$linux$maintainer <- "Martin Frigaard <mjfrigaard@pm.me>"
jsonlite::write_json(pkg, pkg_json, auto_unbox = TRUE, pretty = TRUE)
```

Pop!_OS ships Node.js 18, which is too old. `install_nodejs()` installs a newer version, and `withr::with_path()` puts it ahead of the system version before calling `electron-builder`.

After `sudo dpkg -i`, the 183 MB `.deb` adds **Movie Reviews** to the Applications launcher.

## Recap

The two chapters take `sap` off the server. `webR` and `shinylive` run it in the browser, with a slower first load and code that every user can see. `shinyelectron` turns it into an installer, with `bundled` R on macOS and Windows and `webR` on Linux. Both start from the same launcher `app.R`, and neither changes the package itself.
